opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a harder question than people often assume, because there isn't one single test that settles it. Human intelligence is very broad. We can learn languages, do mathematics, navigate social situations, pick up a new board game from the rules, learn a skill by watching someone, reason about physical objects. So for me, human-level general intelligence means a system that can do the full range of cognitive tasks a typical person can do, and do them at least as well.

What would convince me is when it gets really hard to find counterexamples. Right now you can build a benchmark, the system does well on it, and then someone thinks for a bit and finds a whole class of tasks where it falls over: some kind of reasoning, some kind of learning from experience, keeping track of things over a long period, episodic memory, that sort of thing. Then you add those to the test suite. So I'd want a large, diverse battery of tests covering the breadth of human cognition, and then a serious adversarial effort where people really try to find something a normal human can do that the machine can't. If they put in real effort and keep coming up empty, that's when I'd say we're there.

One thing I'd stress is that it's not just about knowledge. These models already know far more than any individual human. What matters is the flexibility: can it be dropped into a new situation, learn efficiently, and adapt the way a person would? Continual learning, being able to go off and gather information, try things, and actually get better over time. That's a big part of what I'd be looking for.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level general intelligence spans the full range of human cognitive tasks and calls for a large, diverse test battery covering that breadth.

r002.rationale: It proposes a serious adversarial effort to find tasks a normal human can do that the system cannot, even after tasks are added to the test suite.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a good question, and I've thought about it a lot because I've been using the term "AGI" since around 2001, so I feel some responsibility for it.

My rough definition has always been: a system that can do the cognitive tasks that people can typically do. Not the things that the best humans can do, not Einstein, just the kinds of things a normal person can do. That's the bar. So the question becomes, how do you actually test that?

And here I think you have to be careful, because the history of this field is full of people setting a benchmark, a system passing it, and then everyone deciding the benchmark didn't really count. Chess was supposed to require intelligence. Then it didn't. The Turing test was supposed to be the thing, and now we have systems that can fool a lot of people in conversation and nobody thinks that settles it.

So what I'd want is not a single test. I'd want a broad battery. You take a wide range of cognitive tasks that humans can do, a really wide range, and you look at the profile. Does the system have the full breadth, or does it have very spiky capabilities, where it's superhuman in some places and then just falls over on something a child can do? Current systems are very spiky. They can write a decent essay and then fail at something quite simple involving a few steps of reasoning or keeping track of state.

The other thing I'd insist on is adversarial testing. If I just hand you the test set, you can train toward it. What I want is for people who understand the system's weaknesses to go looking for the holes. Can they find tasks that an average person does easily and the system can't? If, after real effort by competent people, they keep failing to find those holes, then I think you're there. That's the bit where I'd actually change my mind.

And I'll add one thing, because I think it gets missed. Part of what makes humans general is learning. Not just performing a task, but picking up a new one from a bit of instruction and a handful of examples, and then getting better at it over time. Episodic memory, continual learning, that sort of thing. A system that has enormous knowledge frozen in at training time but can't do that, I'd still consider it to be missing something important. So I'd want the battery to include tasks where the system has to learn something genuinely new in context, the way a person would on their first day in a job.

If a system did all of that, I'd say, yes, that's human-level AGI. I wouldn't need it to be conscious or to have some mystical spark. I'm quite deflationary about it. If it does the cognitive things people do, broadly, robustly, under adversarial scrutiny, then it's done.

r001.rationale: The response says it would require a broad battery covering a wide range of cognitive tasks and assess whether the system handles them broadly rather than showing spiky abilities.

r002.rationale: It proposes having competent people who understand the system's weaknesses search for tasks an average person can do but the system cannot, even after the system is evaluated across the broad battery.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t look for a single moment or a single test. I’d want a broad collection of evidence that the system can learn and perform across the range of cognitive tasks that humans can do.

The learning part is important. If it does well on tasks it’s been extensively trained on, that tells you something, but I’d also want to put it in unfamiliar situations. Can it work out what’s going on, acquire the skills it needs, and adapt when things change? Can it do that with roughly the amount of experience a human would need?

And we need to be clear about which human we’re comparing it with. Human-level intelligence doesn’t mean being better than every expert at everything. I’d be looking for broadly human-level competence, including the ability to learn new things, rather than a few spectacular capabilities surrounded by limitations that a person would find very easy to overcome.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a broad collection of evidence across the range of cognitive tasks humans can do.

r002.rationale: It recommends testing unfamiliar situations and adaptation, but does not propose adversarially searching for gaps after the system passes a comprehensive test suite.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to see a system that could learn to do the broad range of cognitive tasks that humans can do, including tasks that weren’t anticipated by its developers. You couldn’t convince me with one impressive benchmark score. I’d want a whole body of evidence.

For example, could it encounter a new problem, work out what it needs to learn, acquire that knowledge, and then use it effectively? Could it do that across very different domains, without somebody having to engineer a special solution each time?

And human-level is a little ambiguous, because humans have very different abilities. I wouldn’t require it to beat the best human at everything. But if it could learn and perform competently across roughly the range of intellectual activities that a person can, with comparable opportunities to learn, I’d regard that as strong evidence.

r001.rationale: The candidate says it would require a “whole body of evidence” showing competence across the broad range of human cognitive tasks and varied domains.

r002.rationale: It rejects relying on a single benchmark and calls for broad evidence, but does not propose adversarially searching for gaps after an AI passes a comprehensive test suite.
